title: Fitting a kitchen plinth
subtitle: Measure, cut, and clip or screw kitchen plinths to the base of floor-standing units to close the gap between the cabinet base and the floor
excerpt: How to fit kitchen plinths to floor-standing cabinets. Covers measuring the plinth run, scribing to an uneven floor, cutting corners and ends, and fitting the plinth clips or screwing direct.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK kitchen-fitting trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin panel (typically 150 mm high and 16-18 mm thick MDF or veneered board) that clips to the front of the base-unit legs to close the gap between the cabinet base and the floor. Also called a kickboard or kick-plate. Supplied cut to length or in full-run lengths for site cutting.

A push-fit plastic bracket that snaps onto the adjustable leg of a kitchen base unit and grips the back face of the plinth panel. Allows the plinth to be removed and refitted without tools for access to plumbing or electrical fittings under the cabinet.

content.text: closes the gap under the base units and gives the kitchen its finished base line. The plinth panels push onto
fixed to the unit legs, so they can be removed for access under the cabinets. The main challenge is fitting the plinth to a floor that is not perfectly level.

Snap a plinth clip onto each adjustable leg along the front of the base units. Position the clip with the gripping jaw at the correct height: the front face of the clip should sit 1-2 mm behind the face of the unit doors. For most standard-height base units, the plinth height is 150 mm, so the clip sits 148-150 mm below the underside of the worktop line. Check that the clips are consistent across the whole run.
Measure and cut the plinth lengths

Measure the full run and cut the plinth to length with a hand saw or jigsaw. For an external mitre at a corner (where two runs meet at 90 degrees), cut each end at 45 degrees so the mitre meets neatly. For an internal corner, a butt joint is usually adequate behind the door frame or in a corner that is not directly visible. Cut any shaped end returns with a jigsaw.
Scribe the bottom edge to the floor

If the floor is not level, the plinth will show a gap at the bottom. Hold the plinth in position and check the gap along the base. Use a compass set to the widest gap to scribe a line along the plinth face parallel to the floor. Cut along the scribed line with a jigsaw. The scribed plinth will then follow the floor contour closely. A small gap of 2-3 mm under a plinth is normal and acceptable; it allows floor vapour to ventilate.

Press the plinth panel onto the clips. The panel should clip into each jaw firmly. Check the front face is flush with the doors. If any clip is sitting too far back, remove the plinth and adjust the clip position on the leg. The end of the plinth run at a wall is usually finished with a thin matching end-panel glued to the exposed face.

attrs.symptom: The plinth bows forward away from the units in the middle of a long run
attrs.cause: Not enough clips, or the clips are loose on the legs.
attrs.fix: Add clips at intervals of no more than 500 mm along the run. Ensure each clip is pushed fully onto the leg.

attrs.symptom: Visible gap between two plinth sections at a mitre joint
attrs.cause: The corner is not a true 90 degrees.
attrs.fix: Adjust the mitre angle on one piece slightly. For small gaps, fill with matching silicone sealant or touch up with matching paint.
